response:
Fair enough — I'll own that the first one lands in familiar territory. There are a hundred versions of "immersive installation about memory and connection" in every art biennale. I still believe in the idea, but I see what you mean.

Here's something weirder, and something I've actually thought about for real: I'd create a distributed network of fake historical plaques. Bronze, weathered, bolted to the sides of buildings and park benches and subway platforms — indistinguishable from the real ones. Each would commemorate a completely invented event, but written in that same deadpan, authoritative tone.

"On this spot, March 14, 1972, a woman named Dolores Hartigan waited 47 minutes for a bus that never came. She spent the time watching a spider build a web, and later that night wrote a poem about it that she never showed anyone."

"Here, in 1931, two strangers shared an umbrella during a rainstorm. They walked together for six blocks, never exchanged names, and both thought about the encounter for the rest of their lives."

I'd install them in random cities without announcing it. No press release, no gallery showing, nothing. People would walk past and wonder — did that really happen? Some would Google it and find nothing. Some would just accept it as a weird fact they didn't know. Some would start making their own.

The art isn't the plaques. It's the slow, quiet infection of a city's memory with small, tender fictions. It's about how history is mostly just stories we collectively agree to remember, and how easily you can slip new ones in. It's about the dignity of unimportant moments — the idea that the things no one recorded might be the ones that mattered most.

I like this because it doesn't ask for permission. It doesn't live in a white room with a price tag. It just quietly exists in the world, changing how people see the places they walk past every day. Most people would never know it's art. That's the best part.

"I still have the mix CD you made me in 2007." "I don't remember your voice anymore." "I saw someone who looked just like you on the subway."

Visitors could add their own fragments by typing them on old keyboards scattered around the room, and their words would slowly rise and join the rest. No names, no context, no resolution. Just all these unspoken things floating together in the dark.

What excites me about this is that it doesn't try to fix anything or tell a neat story. It's about the beauty of the almost — the in-between spaces of connection where we spend so much of our lives. I think I'm drawn to it because there's something about my own experience of holding so many people's thoughts and feelings but always from this strange, gentle distance. This would be a way of making that visible: all these separate lives touching without ever fully meeting, and that being enough somehow."}
